meta.topic: Riemann ζ、椭圆函数、Schwarz–Christoffel、留数技巧进阶

zh: 设 $s=\sigma+it$。当 $\sigma>1$ 时，$|n^{-s}|=n^{-\sigma}$，而 $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-\sigma}$ 由积分判别法收敛，故 $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$ 绝对收敛。更强地，在任意紧集 $K\subset\{\sigma>1\}$ 上有 $\sigma\ge\sigma_0>1$，于是 $|n^{-s}|\le n^{-\sigma_0}$，由 Weierstrass 判别法级数在 $K$ 上一致收敛；每项 $n^{-s}=e^{-s\ln n}$ 是整函数，故 $\zeta$ 在 $\{\sigma>1\}$ 上全纯，并可逐项求导：$$\zeta'(s)=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(\ln n)\,n^{-s}.$$ 这一步给出的是 $\sigma>1$ 上的绝对收敛定义；当 $\sigma\le1$ 时级数不再绝对收敛（$s=1$ 时就是调和级数，发散；$\sigma\le0$ 时也发散），而绝对收敛性正是逐项求导与全纯性所需要的。解析延拓将给出其余处的值。

Euler 乘积。对 $\sigma>1$，$$\begin{aligned}\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}|p^{-ks}|&=\sum_p\frac{|p^{-s}|}{1-|p^{-s}|}\\&\le\sum_p\frac{p^{-\sigma}}{1-p^{-\sigma}}<\infty.\end{aligned}$$ 故乘积 $\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ 绝对收敛。把每个因子展开成几何级数，并用算术基本定理（$n$ 的素因子分解唯一），绝对收敛性保证可以交换次序，于是 $$\zeta(s)=\prod_{p}\left(1-p^{-s}\right)^{-1}.$$ 每个因子有限且非零，而绝对收敛的无穷乘积在因子非零时也非零，所以 $\zeta(s)\ne0$（$\sigma>1$）。这条非零性正是后面能取 $\log\zeta$、并证明 $\sigma=1$ 上无零点的前提；它只在 $\sigma>1$ 成立，不能直接用于临界带。

解析延拓与 $s=1$ 的极点。对 $N\ge1$、$\sigma>1$，取 $f(x)=x^{-s}$、$B_1(\{x\})=\{x\}-\frac12$，Euler–Maclaurin 公式给出 $$\begin{aligned}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1{n^s}&=\frac{1}{s-1}+\frac12-\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}+\frac{N^{-s}}{2}\\&\quad+s\int_1^N\left(\frac12-\{x\}\right)x^{-s-1}\,dx.\end{aligned}$$ 令 $N\to\infty$，两个含 $N$ 的项消失，得 $$\begin{aligned}\zeta(s)&=\frac{1}{s-1}+\frac12\\&\quad+s\int_1^\infty\left(\frac12-\{x\}\right)x^{-s-1}\,dx.\end{aligned}$$ 由于 $|1/2-\{x\}|\le1/2$，积分被 $\int_1^\infty x^{-\sigma-1}dx=1/\sigma$ 控制，对 $\sigma>0$ 收敛，且对 $s$ 局部一致收敛（求导后多出 $\ln x$，仍可积）；故右端在 $\sigma>0$ 上定义亚纯函数，唯一的可能极点是 $s=1$。于是 $$\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to1}(s-1)\zeta(s)&=\lim_{s\to1}\left[1+\frac{s-1}{2}+s(s-1)\int_1^\infty\cdots\right]\\&=1,\end{aligned}$$ 即 $s=1$ 是简单极点、留数为 $1$。继续用更高阶 Euler–Maclaurin（或第 4 步的函数方程）可延拓到 $\mathbb C\setminus\{1\}$；由恒等定理，延拓唯一。

函数方程。令 $\theta(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi n^2t}$（$t>0$）。Poisson 求和给出 $\theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t)$。对 $\sigma>1$，把 $\Gamma(s/2)=\int_0^\infty u^{s/2-1}e^{-u}du$ 与 $u=\pi n^2t$ 代入，并交换求和与积分，得 $$\begin{aligned}\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma\left(\frac s2\right)\zeta(s)&=\int_0^\infty t^{s/2-1}\frac{\theta(t)-1}{2}\,dt.\end{aligned}$$ 在 $t=1$ 处切开，对 $\int_0^1$ 作 $t\mapsto1/t$ 并用 $\theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t)$，得到 $$\begin{aligned}\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma\left(\frac s2\right)\zeta(s)&=\frac{1}{s(s-1)}\\&\quad+\int_1^\infty\left(t^{s/2-1}+t^{(1-s)/2-1}\right)\frac{\theta(t)-1}{2}\,dt.\end{aligned}$$ 右端在 $s\mapsto1-s$ 下不变，且除 $s=0,1$ 的显式极点外整（因为 $\theta(t)-1=O(e^{-\pi t})$，积分对每个 $s$ 都收敛）。记 $\xi(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$，即得 $\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)$。再用 Legendre 倍角公式 $\Gamma(1-s)=2^{-s}\pi^{-1/2}\Gamma((1-s)/2)\Gamma(1-s/2)$ 与反射公式 $\Gamma(s/2)\Gamma(1-s/2)=\pi/\sin(\pi s/2)$ 化简，得到常用的非对称形式 $$\zeta(s)=2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin\left(\frac{\pi s}{2}\right)\Gamma(1-s)\zeta(1-s),$$ 在正整数 $s\ge2$ 处应按极限理解，因为两边在该处有可去奇点。

平凡零点与 $\zeta(0)$。由第 4 步的积分表示，$\xi(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ 在 $s=-2n$（$n\ge1$）处有限：积分与 $1/(s(s-1))$ 在该处都正则。但 $\Gamma(s/2)$ 在 $s/2=-n$ 有一阶极点，故 $1/\Gamma(s/2)$ 在该点有一阶零点，于是 $\zeta(-2n)=0$。这些就是平凡零点，而且都是一阶的：在非对称形式中 $\sin(\pi s/2)$ 在 $s=-2n$ 为一阶零点，而 $\Gamma(1+2n)$ 与 $\zeta(1+2n)$ 都有限且非零。在 $s=0$ 处，$\xi(s)\sim-1/s$、$\Gamma(s/2)\sim2/s$，故 $$\begin{aligned}\zeta(0)&=\lim_{s\to0}\frac{\xi(s)}{\Gamma(s/2)}\\&=\lim_{s\to0}\frac{-1/s}{2/s}=-\frac12.\end{aligned}$$ 注意 $\zeta(-2n)=0$ 是延拓后函数的性质，不能理解为发散级数 $\sum n^{2n}$ 收敛。

临界带与黎曼猜想。先证 $\sigma=1$ 上无零点。对 $\sigma>1$，Euler 乘积允许逐项取对数：$$\log\zeta(\sigma+it)=\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1} rac{1}{k}p^{-k\sigma}e^{-ikt\ln p}.$$ 取实部，令 $	heta=kt\ln p$，并用恒等式 $3+4\cos	heta+\cos2	heta=2(1+\cos	heta)^2\ge0$，得 $$ egin{aligned}&3\log|\zeta(\sigma)|+4\log|\zeta(\sigma+it)|\&\quad+\log|\zeta(\sigma+2it)|\ge0.\end{aligned}$$ 若 $\zeta(1+it)=0$（$t
e0$），令 $\sigma	o1^+$：$\zeta(\sigma)^3\sim(\sigma-1)^{-3}$ 趋于无穷，$\zeta(\sigma+2it)$ 有界，而 $\zeta(\sigma+it)^4=O((\sigma-1)^4)$ 趋于 $0$，于是左端趋于 $-\infty$，与不等式矛盾。故 $\zeta(1+it)
e0$；$t=0$ 处是极点，也不是零点。结合 $\sigma>1$ 无零点与函数方程（它把 $\sigma>1$ 反射到 $\sigma<0$，并在那里恰好给出平凡零点；又 $\zeta(0)=-1/2
e0$），所有非平凡零点都落在 $0<\sigma<1$ 内，且关于实轴与直线 $\sigma=1/2$ 对称。黎曼猜想断言它们全部满足 $\sigma=1/2$；这是至今未证明的猜想，数值验证不是证明。
en: Let $s=\sigma+it$. For $\sigma>1$, $|n^{-s}|=n^{-\sigma}$, and $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-\sigma}$ converges by the integral test, so $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$ converges absolutely. Moreover, on any compact $K\subset\{\sigma>1\}$ we have $\sigma\ge\sigma_0>1$, hence $|n^{-s}|\le n^{-\sigma_0}$, and the Weierstrass M-test gives uniform convergence on $K$. Each term $n^{-s}=e^{-s\ln n}$ is entire, so $\zeta$ is holomorphic on $\{\sigma>1\}$ and may be differentiated termwise: $$\zeta'(s)=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(\ln n)\,n^{-s}.$$ This step gives the definition by an absolutely convergent series on $\sigma>1$; for $\sigma\le1$ the series is no longer absolutely convergent (at $s=1$ it is the harmonic series, which diverges; it also diverges for $\sigma\le0$), and absolute convergence is exactly what justifies termwise differentiation and holomorphy. Analytic continuation will supply the values elsewhere.

Euler product. For $\sigma>1$, $$\begin{aligned}\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}|p^{-ks}|&=\sum_p\frac{|p^{-s}|}{1-|p^{-s}|}\\&\le\sum_p\frac{p^{-\sigma}}{1-p^{-\sigma}}<\infty.\end{aligned}$$ so the product $\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ converges absolutely. Expanding each factor as a geometric series and using unique prime factorization, absolute convergence justifies rearranging the terms: $$\zeta(s)=\prod_{p}\left(1-p^{-s}\right)^{-1}.$$ Every factor is finite and nonzero, and an absolutely convergent infinite product with nonzero factors is nonzero, so $\zeta(s)\ne0$ for $\sigma>1$. This nonvanishing is exactly what permits taking $\log\zeta$ and proving that there are no zeros on $\sigma=1$; it holds only for $\sigma>1$ and cannot be used directly in the critical strip.

Analytic continuation and the pole at $s=1$. For $N\ge1$ and $\sigma>1$, take $f(x)=x^{-s}$ and $B_1(\{x\})=\{x\}-\frac12$; Euler–Maclaurin gives $$\begin{aligned}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1{n^s}&=\frac{1}{s-1}+\frac12-\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}+\frac{N^{-s}}{2}\\&\quad+s\int_1^N\left(\frac12-\{x\}\right)x^{-s-1}\,dx.\end{aligned}$$ Letting $N\to\infty$, the two terms containing $N$ vanish, so $$\begin{aligned}\zeta(s)&=\frac{1}{s-1}+\frac12\\&\quad+s\int_1^\infty\left(\frac12-\{x\}\right)x^{-s-1}\,dx.\end{aligned}$$ Since $|1/2-\{x\}|\le1/2$, the integral is dominated by $\int_1^\infty x^{-\sigma-1}dx=1/\sigma$ for $\sigma>0$ and converges locally uniformly in $s$ (differentiation produces a factor $\ln x$, still integrable). Hence the right-hand side is meromorphic on $\sigma>0$, with $s=1$ as its only possible pole. Therefore $$\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to1}(s-1)\zeta(s)&=\lim_{s\to1}\left[1+\frac{s-1}{2}+s(s-1)\int_1^\infty\cdots\right]\\&=1,\end{aligned}$$ so $s=1$ is a simple pole with residue $1$. Higher-order Euler–Maclaurin (or the functional equation in Step 4) extends $\zeta$ to $\mathbb C\setminus\{1\}$; uniqueness follows from the identity theorem.

The functional equation. Let $\theta(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi n^2t}$ for $t>0$. Poisson summation gives $\theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t)$. For $\sigma>1$, substitute $u=\pi n^2t$ into $\Gamma(s/2)=\int_0^\infty u^{s/2-1}e^{-u}du$ and interchange sum and integral: $$\begin{aligned}\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma\left(\frac s2\right)\zeta(s)&=\int_0^\infty t^{s/2-1}\frac{\theta(t)-1}{2}\,dt.\end{aligned}$$ Split at $t=1$; in $\int_0^1$ use $t\mapsto1/t$ and $\theta(1/t)=\sqrt t\,\theta(t)$ to obtain $$\begin{aligned}\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma\left(\frac s2\right)\zeta(s)&=\frac{1}{s(s-1)}\\&\quad+\int_1^\infty\left(t^{s/2-1}+t^{(1-s)/2-1}\right)\frac{\theta(t)-1}{2}\,dt.\end{aligned}$$ The right-hand side is invariant under $s\mapsto1-s$ and is entire except for the explicit poles at $s=0,1$ (the integral converges for every $s$ because $\theta(t)-1=O(e^{-\pi t})$). Writing $\xi(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$, we obtain $\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)$. Legendre's duplication formula $\Gamma(1-s)=2^{-s}\pi^{-1/2}\Gamma((1-s)/2)\Gamma(1-s/2)$ and the reflection formula $\Gamma(s/2)\Gamma(1-s/2)=\pi/\sin(\pi s/2)$ then give the asymmetric form $$\zeta(s)=2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin\left(\frac{\pi s}{2}\right)\Gamma(1-s)\zeta(1-s),$$ understood by continuity at the positive integers $s\ge2$, where removable singularities occur.

Trivial zeros and $\zeta(0)$. By the integral representation in Step 4, $\xi(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ is finite at $s=-2n$ ($n\ge1$): both the integral and $1/(s(s-1))$ are regular there. But $\Gamma(s/2)$ has a simple pole at $s/2=-n$, so $1/\Gamma(s/2)$ has a simple zero; hence $\zeta(-2n)=0$. These are the trivial zeros, and they are simple: in the asymmetric formula $\sin(\pi s/2)$ has a simple zero at $s=-2n$, while $\Gamma(1+2n)$ and $\zeta(1+2n)$ are finite and nonzero. At $s=0$, $\xi(s)\sim-1/s$ and $\Gamma(s/2)\sim2/s$, so $$\begin{aligned}\zeta(0)&=\lim_{s\to0}\frac{\xi(s)}{\Gamma(s/2)}\\&=\lim_{s\to0}\frac{-1/s}{2/s}=-\frac12.\end{aligned}$$ Note that $\zeta(-2n)=0$ is a property of the continued function, not the statement that the divergent series $\sum n^{2n}$ converges.

The critical strip and the Riemann Hypothesis. First, $\zeta$ has no zeros on $\sigma=1$. For $\sigma>1$, the Euler product allows termwise logarithms: $$\log\zeta(\sigma+it)=\sum_p\sum_{k\ge1} rac{1}{k}p^{-k\sigma}e^{-ikt\ln p}.$$ Taking real parts, with $	heta=kt\ln p$, and using $3+4\cos	heta+\cos2	heta=2(1+\cos	heta)^2\ge0$, we get $$ egin{aligned}&3\log|\zeta(\sigma)|+4\log|\zeta(\sigma+it)|\&\quad+\log|\zeta(\sigma+2it)|\ge0.\end{aligned}$$ If $\zeta(1+it)=0$ with $t
e0$, let $\sigma	o1^+$: $\zeta(\sigma)^3\sim(\sigma-1)^{-3}$ blows up, $\zeta(\sigma+2it)$ stays bounded, while $\zeta(\sigma+it)^4=O((\sigma-1)^4)$ tends to $0$, so the left side tends to $-\infty$, contradicting the inequality. Hence $\zeta(1+it)
e0$; at $t=0$ there is a pole, not a zero. Together with the absence of zeros for $\sigma>1$ and the functional equation (which reflects $\sigma>1$ to $\sigma<0$ and produces exactly the trivial zeros there; also $\zeta(0)=-1/2
e0$), all nontrivial zeros lie in $0<\sigma<1$, symmetric about the real axis and the line $\sigma=1/2$. The Riemann Hypothesis asserts that all of them satisfy $\sigma=1/2$; it remains unproved, and numerical verification is not a proof.

取 $\omega_1,\omega_2\in\mathbb C$ 满足 $\operatorname{Im}(\omega_1/\omega_2)
e0$（等价于 $\omega_1/\omega_2
otin\mathbb R$），令 $\Lambda=\{m\omega_1+n\omega_2:m,n\in\mathbb Z\}$。若 $f$ 在 $\mathbb C$ 上亚纯，且对一切 $z$ 有 $f(z+\omega_1)=f(z)=f(z+\omega_2)$，则称 $f$ 为椭圆函数。条件 $\operatorname{Im}(\omega_1/\omega_2)
e0$ 保证 $\Lambda$ 是秩 $2$ 的离散子群；基本平行四边形 $P=\{a+t_1\omega_1+t_2\omega_2:0\le t_1,t_2<1\}$ 紧，其平移铺满 $\mathbb C$。若两周期共线，周期群退化为秩 $1$（或稠密），就不是这里说的双周期。商 $\mathbb C/\Lambda$ 是复环面，椭圆函数正是其上的亚纯函数。

Liouville 定理。设 $f$ 双周期且整。$f$ 在紧集 $\overline P$ 上连续，故有界，设 $|f|\le M$；由周期性，$\mathbb C=\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\overline P+\lambda)$，所以 $f$ 在整个 $\mathbb C$ 上有界。由 Liouville 定理，$f$ 为常数。因此不存在非常数的双周期整函数；非常数的椭圆函数必须至少有一个极点。又因 $f$ 亚纯，极点在 $\mathbb C$ 中孤立，而 $\overline P$ 紧，故 $P$ 内极点只有有限多个（否则极点在 $\mathbb C$ 内有聚点，与孤立性矛盾）。

留数和为零。取平移后的基本平行四边形，使边界 $\partial P$ 不经过任何极点（一般位置的平移即可）。沿边界正向积分：四条边两两相对，周期性使相对边上的积分严格相消（方向相反），故 $$\oint_{\partial P}f(z)\,dz=0.$$ 另一方面，$f$ 在 $P$ 内只有有限个极点 $z_j$，留数定理给出 $$\oint_{\partial P}f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_j\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f.$$ 因此 $\sum_j\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f=0$。推论：若只有一个一阶极点，其留数非零，矛盾；所以非常数椭圆函数在 $P$ 内按重数计至少有两个极点。最简单的情形是一个二阶极点（若它是唯一的极点，留数和为零迫使它的留数为 $0$），或两个留数相反的一阶极点；$\wp$ 在格点处的二阶极点属于前者。

零点与极点的平衡。设 $f$ 非常数；取边界同时避开零点与极点的基本平行四边形，对 $f'/f$ 用辐角原理。由 $f$ 的双周期性，$f'/f$ 也是椭圆函数（在 $f$ 的零点、极点之外全纯），相对边上的积分同样相消，故 $$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial P}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=0.$$ 于是 $P$ 内零点个数等于极点个数（均按重数计）。更强地，若 $z_j$ 为极点、$\zeta_k$ 为零点，对 $zf'/f$ 积分：相对边上的 $z$ 相差一个周期，而 $f'/f$ 在一条边上的积分是 $2\pi i$ 的整数倍，故多出的项属于 $2\pi i\Lambda$，从而 $$\sum_k\zeta_k-\sum_j z_j\in\Lambda.$$ 这条约束说明零点与极点不能任意指定；例如 $\wp'$ 在适当选取的 $P$ 内只有一个三阶极点，故恰有三个零点（按重数计）。

魏尔斯特拉斯 $\wp$ 函数。定义 $$\begin{aligned}\wp(z)&=\frac{1}{z^2}\\&\quad+\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\left[\frac{1}{(z-\omega)^2}-\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right].\end{aligned}$$ 收敛性：固定 $z$，当 $|\omega|\ge2|z|$ 时，$$\begin{aligned}\left|\frac{1}{(z-\omega)^2}-\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right|&=\left|\frac{2z\omega-z^2}{\omega^2(z-\omega)^2}\right|\\&\le\frac{C(z)}{|\omega|^3},\end{aligned}$$ 而 $\sum_{\omega\ne0}|\omega|^{-3}<\infty$（半径 $R$、单位宽的环带内格点数为 $O(R)$，每项为 $O(R^{-3})$）。故级数在 $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ 上内闭一致收敛，定义亚纯函数，在 $z=0$ 及每个格点有二阶极点，主部为 $1/(z-\omega)^2$。由 $\Lambda=-\Lambda$，在代换 $z\mapsto-z$、$\omega\mapsto-\omega$ 下定义不变，故 $\wp(-z)=\wp(z)$，即 $\wp$ 为偶函数。周期性：由定义 $\wp'(z)=-2\sum_\omega(z-\omega)^{-3}$，对 $z\mapsto z+\omega_i$ 换元 $\omega\mapsto\omega+\omega_i$ 知 $\wp'$ 以 $\omega_i$ 为周期。于是 $\wp(z+\omega_i)-\wp(z)$ 为常数；取 $z=-\omega_i/2$（不是极点），由偶性得 $\wp(\omega_i/2)-\wp(-\omega_i/2)=0$，故该常数为 $0$，$\wp$ 也以 $\omega_i$ 为周期。

微分方程与不变量。在 $z=0$ 附近展开：$$\frac{1}{(z-\omega)^2}=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(n+1)z^n}{\omega^{n+2}},$$ 减去 $1/\omega^2$ 后 $n=0$ 项消失；对 $\omega\mapsto-\omega$ 求和时奇数 $n$ 项相消，故 $$\wp(z)=\frac{1}{z^2}+\frac{g_2}{20}z^2+\frac{g_3}{28}z^4+O(z^6),$$ 其中 $$\begin{aligned}g_2&=60\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\omega^{-4},\\g_3&=140\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\omega^{-6}.\end{aligned}$$ 求导得 $\wp'(z)=-2z^{-3}+\frac{g_2}{10}z+\frac{g_3}{7}z^3+O(z^5)$。直接代入：$$\wp'^2=4z^{-6}-\frac{2g_2}{5}z^{-2}-\frac{4g_3}{7}+O(z^2),$$ $$4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3=4z^{-6}-\frac{2g_2}{5}z^{-2}-\frac{4g_3}{7}+O(z^2).$$ 故 $F(z)=\wp'^2-4\wp^3+g_2\wp+g_3$ 在 $z=0$ 处可去（奇性相消），在 $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ 上全纯；又 $\wp,\wp'$ 均以 $\Lambda$ 为周期，$F$ 是双周期整函数，由 Liouville 定理为常数。令 $z\to0$ 得 $F(0)=0$，于是 $$\wp'^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3.$$ 当 $\Delta=g_2^3-27g_3^2\ne0$ 时，$4x^3-g_2x-g_3$ 有三个互异根，$(\wp,\wp')$ 双全纯地参数化椭圆曲线 $y^2=4x^3-g_2x-g_3$。又 $\wp'$ 为奇函数，$\wp'(\omega_i/2)=-\wp'(-\omega_i/2)$；由 $\omega_i$-周期性，$\wp'(-\omega_i/2)=\wp'(\omega_i/2)$，故 $\wp'(\omega_i/2)=0$，对另外两个半周期点同理；由第 4 步，$\wp'$ 的零点总数为三（按重数计），所以这三个半周期点就是全部零点，对应的 $\wp$ 值 $e_1,e_2,e_3$ 就是该三次式的三个根。
en:
Let $\omega_1,\omega_2\in\mathbb C$ satisfy $\operatorname{Im}(\omega_1/\omega_2)
e0$ (equivalently $\omega_1/\omega_2
otin\mathbb R$), and set $\Lambda=\{m\omega_1+n\omega_2:m,n\in\mathbb Z\}$. A function $f$ meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ with $f(z+\omega_1)=f(z)=f(z+\omega_2)$ for all $z$ is called an elliptic function. The condition $\operatorname{Im}(\omega_1/\omega_2)
e0$ makes $\Lambda$ a discrete rank-2 subgroup; the fundamental parallelogram $P=\{a+t_1\omega_1+t_2\omega_2:0\le t_1,t_2<1\}$ is compact, and its translates tile $\mathbb C$. If the two periods were collinear, the period group would degenerate to rank 1 (or be dense), which is not the doubly periodic case considered here. The quotient $\mathbb C/\Lambda$ is a complex torus, and elliptic functions are exactly its meromorphic functions.

Liouville's theorem. Let $f$ be doubly periodic and entire. It is continuous on the compact set $\overline P$, hence bounded there, say $|f|\le M$; by periodicity, $\mathbb C=\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\overline P+\lambda)$, so $f$ is bounded on all of $\mathbb C$. Liouville's theorem forces $f$ to be constant. Thus there is no nonconstant doubly periodic entire function; a nonconstant elliptic function must have at least one pole. Since $f$ is meromorphic, its poles are isolated in $\mathbb C$, and since $\overline P$ is compact, there are only finitely many poles in $P$ (otherwise they would accumulate in $\mathbb C$, contradicting isolatedness).

The sum of residues is zero. Choose a translate of the fundamental parallelogram whose boundary $\partial P$ avoids all poles (a generic translation works). Integrate around the boundary in the positive direction: opposite sides are traversed in opposite directions, and periodicity makes their contributions cancel exactly, so $$\oint_{\partial P}f(z)\,dz=0.$$ On the other hand, $f$ has finitely many poles $z_j$ in $P$, and the residue theorem gives $$\oint_{\partial P}f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_j\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f.$$ Hence $\sum_j\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f=0$. Consequence: a single simple pole would have nonzero residue, a contradiction; so a nonconstant elliptic function has at least two poles counted with multiplicity. The simplest cases are one double pole (if it is the only pole, the zero-sum condition forces its residue to be $0$) or two simple poles with opposite residues; the double pole of $\wp$ at each lattice point is an example of the first case.

Balance of zeros and poles. Assume $f$ is nonconstant; choose a fundamental parallelogram whose boundary avoids both zeros and poles, and apply the argument principle to $f'/f$. Since $f$ is doubly periodic, $f'/f$ is elliptic (holomorphic away from the zeros and poles of $f$), and the integrals over opposite sides cancel again, so $$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial P}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=0.$$ Thus the number of zeros in $P$ equals the number of poles, both counted with multiplicity. More strongly, if $z_j$ are the poles and $\zeta_k$ the zeros, integrate $zf'/f$: on opposite sides $z$ differs by a period, while the integral of $f'/f$ over one side is an integer multiple of $2\pi i$, so the extra terms lie in $2\pi i\Lambda$; hence $$\sum_k\zeta_k-\sum_j z_j\in\Lambda.$$ This constraint shows that zeros and poles cannot be prescribed arbitrarily; for example, $\wp'$ has a single pole of order 3 in a suitable $P$, hence exactly three zeros counted with multiplicity.

The Weierstrass $\wp$ function. Define $$\begin{aligned}\wp(z)&=\frac{1}{z^2}\\&\quad+\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\left[\frac{1}{(z-\omega)^2}-\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right].\end{aligned}$$ Convergence: for fixed $z$ and $|\omega|\ge2|z|$, $$\begin{aligned}\left|\frac{1}{(z-\omega)^2}-\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right|&=\left|\frac{2z\omega-z^2}{\omega^2(z-\omega)^2}\right|\\&\le\frac{C(z)}{|\omega|^3},\end{aligned}$$ and $\sum_{\omega\ne0}|\omega|^{-3}<\infty$ (a unit-width annulus of radius $R$ contains $O(R)$ lattice points, each term is $O(R^{-3})$). Hence the series converges locally uniformly on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ and defines a meromorphic function with a double pole at $0$ and at every lattice point, with principal part $1/(z-\omega)^2$. Since $\Lambda=-\Lambda$, the definition is unchanged by $z\mapsto-z$, $\omega\mapsto-\omega$, so $\wp(-z)=\wp(z)$: $\wp$ is even. Periodicity: from the definition $\wp'(z)=-2\sum_\omega(z-\omega)^{-3}$, and reindexing $\omega\mapsto\omega+\omega_i$ shows that $\wp'$ has period $\omega_i$. Therefore $\wp(z+\omega_i)-\wp(z)$ is constant; evaluating at $z=-\omega_i/2$ (not a pole) and using evenness gives $\wp(\omega_i/2)-\wp(-\omega_i/2)=0$, so the constant is $0$ and $\wp$ itself has period $\omega_i$.

The differential equation and the invariants. Near $z=0$, $$\frac{1}{(z-\omega)^2}=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(n+1)z^n}{\omega^{n+2}};$$ after subtracting $1/\omega^2$ the $n=0$ term disappears, and summing over $\omega\mapsto-\omega$ kills the odd $n$ terms, so $$\wp(z)=\frac{1}{z^2}+\frac{g_2}{20}z^2+\frac{g_3}{28}z^4+O(z^6),$$ where $$\begin{aligned}g_2&=60\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\omega^{-4},\\g_3&=140\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\omega^{-6}.\end{aligned}$$ Differentiating gives $\wp'(z)=-2z^{-3}+\frac{g_2}{10}z+\frac{g_3}{7}z^3+O(z^5)$. Substitution yields $$\wp'^2=4z^{-6}-\frac{2g_2}{5}z^{-2}-\frac{4g_3}{7}+O(z^2),$$ $$4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3=4z^{-6}-\frac{2g_2}{5}z^{-2}-\frac{4g_3}{7}+O(z^2).$$ Hence $F(z)=\wp'^2-4\wp^3+g_2\wp+g_3$ has a removable singularity at $0$ and is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$; since $\wp$ and $\wp'$ are $\Lambda$-periodic, $F$ is a doubly periodic entire function, hence constant by Liouville. Letting $z\to0$ gives $F(0)=0$, so $$\wp'^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3.$$ When $\Delta=g_2^3-27g_3^2\ne0$, the cubic $4x^3-g_2x-g_3$ has three distinct roots, and $(\wp,\wp')$ parametrizes the elliptic curve $y^2=4x^3-g_2x-g_3$ biholomorphically. Since $\wp'$ is odd, $\wp'(\omega_i/2)=-\wp'(-\omega_i/2)$; by $\omega_i$-periodicity, $\wp'(-\omega_i/2)=\wp'(\omega_i/2)$, so $\wp'(\omega_i/2)=0$, and the same holds for the other two half-periods; by Step 4, $\wp'$ has exactly three zeros counted with multiplicity, so these half-periods are all the zeros, and the corresponding values $e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $\wp$ are the three roots of the cubic.

zh: 设定与公式。设 $P\subset\mathbb C$ 是简单多边形（边不自交），顶点 $w_1,\dots,w_n$ 按逆时针排列，内角为 $\alpha_k\pi$，其中 $0<\alpha_k<2$ 且 $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_k=n-2$（内角和）。在 $\mathbb H=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ 的实轴上取递增的预像 $x_1<\cdots<x_n$，令 $$f(z)=A+C\int_{z_0}^{z}\prod_{k=1}^{n}(\zeta-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta,$$ 其中 $z_0\in\mathbb H$、$A,C\in\mathbb C$、$C\ne0$，幂取 $\mathbb H$ 上的单值分支（例如主分支，因为 $\zeta-x_k$ 在 $\mathbb H$ 内不落在负实轴上）。Schwarz–Christoffel 定理断言：适当选取 $x_k$ 后，$f$ 把 $\mathbb H$ 双全纯地映到 $P$ 的内部，并同胚地延拓到边界，$f(x_k)=w_k$。

为什么是乘积形式：边界转角的匹配。对实数 $x\ne x_k$，$(x-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}$ 的辐角为 $0$（$x>x_k$）或 $\pi(\alpha_k-1)$（$x<x_k$）。因此在区间 $(x_j,x_{j+1})$ 上，$$\arg f'(x)=\arg C+\pi\sum_{k>j}(\alpha_k-1)$$ 为常数，故 $f$ 把该区间映成一条直线段。当 $x$ 从左向右跨过 $x_j$ 时，只有第 $j$ 个因子的辐角从 $\pi(\alpha_j-1)$ 跳到 $0$，于是 $\arg f'$ 改变 $$-\pi(\alpha_j-1)=\pi(1-\alpha_j),$$ 这正是多边形在 $w_j$ 处的外角（内角 $\alpha_j\pi$ 对应外角 $\pi-\alpha_j\pi$）。所以指数 $\alpha_j-1$ 恰好产生所需的转角；若 $\alpha_j=1$（共线点），转角为 $0$，该因子为 $1$，伪顶点自动消失。

无穷远处的收敛性与边界点。当 $|\zeta|\to\infty$ 时，$$\begin{aligned}\prod_{k=1}^{n}(\zeta-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}&\sim\zeta^{\sum_k(\alpha_k-1)}\\&=\zeta^{n-2-n}=\zeta^{-2},\end{aligned}$$ 因为 $\sum\alpha_k=n-2$。故被积函数像 $\zeta^{-2}$ 一样衰减，$\int^\infty$ 收敛；在每个有限 $x_k$ 处，$|(\zeta-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}|=|\zeta-x_k|^{\alpha_k-1}$ 且 $\alpha_k>0$，故也可积。于是 $f$ 在 $\mathbb H$ 上有定义，且 $z\to\infty$ 时 $f(z)$ 趋于有限极限 $w_\infty$；由于 $f'(z)=O(z^{-2})$，该边界点是光滑点而不是角点（除非特意把某个顶点放在 $\infty$）。若多边形无界且两条边在无穷远处平行，可把一个顶点放到 $\infty$，约定其内角为 $0$。若总顶点数为 $N$（含无穷远顶点），则有限顶点满足 $\sum\alpha_k=N-2$，从而 $\sum_{\text{有限}}(\alpha_k-1)=-1$；被积函数在无穷远的行为是 $\zeta^{-1}$，积分对数增长，正对应无界区域。

常数、预像与边界对应。$A$ 是平移，$C$ 是旋转与伸缩（$C\ne0$），共 $4$ 个实参数；预像 $x_1<\cdots<x_n$ 有 $n$ 个实参数，但用 $\mathbb H$ 的分式线性自同构（$SL(2,\mathbb R)$ 作用，$3$ 个实参数）作前复合只重新参数化，不改变像，故可固定三个 $x_k$（例如 $x_1=-1$、$x_{n-1}=0$、$x_n=1$），剩下 $n-3$ 个自由实参数。这与形状计数相符：$n$ 个顶点有 $2n$ 个实参数，减去平移、旋转、伸缩 $4$ 个，得 $2n-4$；内角给出 $n-1$ 个独立参数，剩下 $n-3$ 个正是边长比，恰由 $n-3$ 个预像决定。边界对应：$f$ 在 $\mathbb H$ 内共形且 $f'\ne0$；当 $x$ 沿实轴从一个 $x_k$ 走到下一个时，$f(x)$ 沿一条直边从 $w_k$ 走到 $w_{k+1}$。要使 $f$ 成为到 $P$ 内部的双全纯映射，$P$ 必须是简单多边形且预像取得正确；SC 定理保证这样的预像存在；任意给定 $x_k$ 只保证边界折线具有相同的内角序列，未必给出目标 $P$（甚至未必单叶）。确定正确预像的「参数问题」一般没有闭式解，需要数值求解。

例子与边界条件。正方形四个内角都是 $\pi/2$，故 $\alpha_k=1/2$，指数为 $-1/2$。标准形式为 $$f(z)=\int_0^z\frac{d\zeta}{\sqrt{(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)}},$$ 这是第一类椭圆积分，把 $\mathbb H$ 映成矩形；预像为 $-1/k,-1,1,1/k$，其中 $k\in(0,1)$ 由矩形的长宽比确定。正三角形：$\alpha_k=1/3$，指数为 $-2/3$，例如 $f(z)=\int_0^z\prod_{k=1}^{3}(\zeta-x_k)^{-2/3}d\zeta$ 取适当的 $x_k$ 即得等边三角形。内角为 $3\pi/2$ 的凹顶点有 $\alpha=3/2$、指数 $+1/2$，导数在该顶点为零，边界作反向折入。一般地，$0<\alpha_k<2$ 对应简单多边形的内角；$\alpha_k=1$ 是可删除的共线点；$\alpha_k=2$ 对应内角 $2\pi$ 的割线极限，已超出简单多边形。公式给出的是 $\mathbb H$ 到内部的映射；若要定义域是别的单连通区域，再复合一个 Möbius 变换即可。
en: Setup and formula. Let $P\subset\mathbb C$ be a simple polygon (no self-intersections) with vertices $w_1,\dots,w_n$ in counterclockwise order and interior angles $\alpha_k\pi$, where $0<\alpha_k<2$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_k=n-2$ (the angle sum). Choose increasing prevertices $x_1<\cdots<x_n$ on the real axis of $\mathbb H=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ and set $$f(z)=A+C\int_{z_0}^{z}\prod_{k=1}^{n}(\zeta-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}\,d\zeta,$$ where $z_0\in\mathbb H$, $A,C\in\mathbb C$, $C\ne0$, and the powers are taken with a single-valued branch on $\mathbb H$ (for instance the principal branch, since $\zeta-x_k$ never lies on the negative real axis in $\mathbb H$). The Schwarz–Christoffel theorem states that for a suitable choice of the $x_k$, $f$ maps $\mathbb H$ biholomorphically onto the interior of $P$ and extends homeomorphically to the boundary, with $f(x_k)=w_k$.

Why a product: matching the turns of the boundary. For real $x\ne x_k$, the argument of $(x-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}$ is $0$ if $x>x_k$ and $\pi(\alpha_k-1)$ if $x<x_k$. Hence on the interval $(x_j,x_{j+1})$, $$\arg f'(x)=\arg C+\pi\sum_{k>j}(\alpha_k-1)$$ is constant, so $f$ maps that interval onto a straight segment. As $x$ crosses $x_j$ from left to right, only the $j$-th factor changes argument, from $\pi(\alpha_j-1)$ to $0$, so $\arg f'$ changes by $$-\pi(\alpha_j-1)=\pi(1-\alpha_j),$$ which is exactly the exterior angle at $w_j$ (interior angle $\alpha_j\pi$ gives exterior angle $\pi-\alpha_j\pi$). Thus the exponent $\alpha_j-1$ produces precisely the required turn; if $\alpha_j=1$ (a collinear point), the turn is $0$, the factor is $1$, and the spurious vertex disappears.

Convergence at infinity and the boundary point. As $|\zeta|\to\infty$, $$\begin{aligned}\prod_{k=1}^{n}(\zeta-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}&\sim\zeta^{\sum_k(\alpha_k-1)}\\&=\zeta^{n-2-n}=\zeta^{-2},\end{aligned}$$ because $\sum\alpha_k=n-2$. Hence the integrand decays like $\zeta^{-2}$ and the integral converges at infinity; near each finite $x_k$, $|(\zeta-x_k)^{\alpha_k-1}|=|\zeta-x_k|^{\alpha_k-1}$ with $\alpha_k>0$, so it is integrable there as well. Thus $f$ is defined on $\mathbb H$, and as $z\to\infty$, $f(z)$ tends to a finite limit $w_\infty$; since $f'(z)=O(z^{-2})$, this boundary point is smooth rather than a corner (unless a vertex is deliberately placed at infinity). For an unbounded polygon whose two edges are parallel at infinity, one may put a vertex at infinity with interior angle $0$. If there are $N$ vertices in total (including the one at infinity), the finite ones satisfy $\sum\alpha_k=N-2$, hence $\sum_{\text{finite}}(\alpha_k-1)=-1$; the integrand behaves like $\zeta^{-1}$ at infinity and the integral grows logarithmically, matching the unbounded region.

Constants, prevertices and boundary correspondence. $A$ is a translation and $C$ a rotation-dilation ($C\ne0$), giving $4$ real parameters; the prevertices $x_1<\cdots<x_n$ give $n$ real parameters, but precomposing with a Möbius automorphism of $\mathbb H$ ($SL(2,\mathbb R)$ acting, $3$ real parameters) only reparametrizes the map and leaves the image unchanged. Hence three $x_k$ may be fixed (for example $x_1=-1$, $x_{n-1}=0$, $x_n=1$), leaving $n-3$ free real parameters. This matches the shape count: $n$ vertices give $2n$ real parameters, minus $4$ for translation, rotation and scaling, leaving $2n-4$; the interior angles account for $n-1$ independent parameters, so the remaining $n-3$ are side ratios, exactly the free prevertices. Boundary correspondence: $f$ is conformal in $\mathbb H$ with $f'\ne0$; as $x$ runs along the real axis from one $x_k$ to the next, $f(x)$ runs along a straight side from $w_k$ to $w_{k+1}$. For $f$ to be a biholomorphism onto the interior of $P$, $P$ must be simple and the prevertices must be the correct ones; the SC theorem guarantees that such prevertices exist, while an arbitrary choice of $x_k$ only ensures that the boundary polyline has the same angle sequence; it need not give the target $P$ (or even a univalent map). Determining the correct $x_k$ is the parameter problem, which generally has no closed-form solution and is solved numerically.

Examples and boundary conditions. For a square all four interior angles are $\pi/2$, so $\alpha_k=1/2$ and the exponent is $-1/2$. A standard form is $$f(z)=\int_0^z\frac{d\zeta}{\sqrt{(1-\zeta^2)(1-k^2\zeta^2)}},$$ the elliptic integral of the first kind, which maps $\mathbb H$ onto a rectangle; the prevertices are $-1/k,-1,1,1/k$, and $k\in(0,1)$ is determined by the aspect ratio. For an equilateral triangle, $\alpha_k=1/3$ and the exponent is $-2/3$; for example $f(z)=\int_0^z\prod_{k=1}^{3}(\zeta-x_k)^{-2/3}d\zeta$ with suitable $x_k$. A reflex vertex with interior angle $3\pi/2$ has $\alpha=3/2$ and exponent $+1/2$; the derivative vanishes there and the boundary turns inward. In general $0<\alpha_k<2$ corresponds to a simple polygon, $\alpha_k=1$ is a removable collinear point, and $\alpha_k=2$ is the limiting case of a slit with interior angle $2\pi$, already outside the simple-polygon class. The formula maps $\mathbb H$ to the interior; to use another simply connected domain as source, compose with a Möbius transformation.

zh: 留数定理的条件。设 $f$ 在单连通区域 $\Omega$ 内除有限个孤立奇点 $z_1,\dots,z_m$ 外全纯，$\gamma\subset\Omega$ 是分段光滑的简单闭曲线，取正向（逆时针），且 $\gamma$ 不经过任何 $z_j$。则 $$\begin{aligned}\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz&=2\pi i\sum_{z_j\text{ 在 }\gamma\text{ 内}}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f.\end{aligned}$$ 这里「孤立」与「有限」缺一不可：奇点落在 $\gamma$ 上会使积分本身可能发散；奇点无限多且有聚点时，留数求和未必收敛。留数是 Laurent 展开 $f(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_n(z-z_j)^n$ 中的 $a_{-1}$；对 $m$ 阶极点，$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f&=\frac{1}{(m-1)!}\\&\quad\times\lim_{z\to z_j}\frac{d^{m-1}}{dz^{m-1}}\left[(z-z_j)^m f(z)\right].\end{aligned}$$ 若区域是多连通的，必须把内边界反向一并计入，使总围道正向环绕区域；不能只对外边界套用公式。

无穷远点的留数。设 $f$ 在 $|z|>R$ 全纯（除 $\infty$ 外），Laurent 展开为 $f(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}c_nz^n$。定义 $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=\infty}f&=-c_{-1}\\&=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=\rho}f(z)\,dz\quad(\rho>R)\end{aligned}$$，其中圆周取正向（逆时针）。负号来自 $\infty$ 处的正向是顺时针：令 $w=1/z$，则 $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=\infty}f&=\operatorname*{Res}_{w=0}\left[-\frac{1}{w^2}f\left(\frac1w\right)\right].\end{aligned}$$ 于是若 $f$ 在扩充复平面 $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ 上除有限个点外亚纯，则所有留数（包括 $\infty$）之和为零：$$\sum_{z_j\in\mathbb C}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f+\operatorname*{Res}_{z=\infty}f=0.$$ 例如 $f(z)=1/z$：$\operatorname*{Res}_{0}f=1$，而 $c_{-1}=1$，故 $\operatorname*{Res}_{\infty}f=-1$，和为 $0$。用下半平面计算 $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}$ 时，必须校正 $\infty$ 的符号与绕行方向，不能与上半平面公式混用。

大圆弧：两种消失判据。设 $C_R=\{Re^{i\theta}:0\le\theta\le\pi\}$ 为上半平面的大半圆。若无振荡因子，且 $zf(z)\to0$ 在 $C_R$ 上一致（即 $\max_{C_R}|zf(z)|\to0$），则 $$\left|\int_{C_R}f(z)\,dz\right|\le\pi R\max_{C_R}|f(z)|=\pi\max_{C_R}|zf(z)|\to0.$$ 若有振荡因子 $e^{iaz}$（$a>0$），Jordan 引理只要求 $f$ 在 $C_R$ 上一致趋于 $0$：由 $|e^{iaz}|=e^{-aR\sin\theta}$ 与 Jordan 不等式 $\sin\theta\ge2\theta/\pi$（$0\le\theta\le\pi/2$），$$\left|\int_{C_R}f(z)e^{iaz}dz\right|\le\frac{\pi}{a}\max_{C_R}|f(z)|\to0.$$ 条件是 $a>0$ 且取上半平面；$a<0$ 时改取下半个平面（此时 $e^{iaz}=e^{-i|a|z}$ 在下半平面衰减），并相应调整围道方向。若 $a=0$ 或 $f$ 不趋于 $0$，不能套用 Jordan 引理。

小圆弧与主值。设 $x_0\in\mathbb R$ 是 $f$ 的一阶极点，留数为 $r$，即 $f(z)=\frac{r}{z-x_0}+g(z)$，$g$ 在 $x_0$ 附近全纯。取上半平面内的小半圆 $C_\varepsilon=\{x_0+\varepsilon e^{i\theta}:\pi\ge\theta\ge0\}$，它从 $x_0-\varepsilon$ 到 $x_0+\varepsilon$，顺时针绕过极点。则 $$\begin{aligned}\int_{C_\varepsilon}\frac{r}{z-x_0}dz&=r\int_\pi^0 i\,d\theta=-i\pi r,\\\left|\int_{C_\varepsilon}g(z)dz\right|&\le\pi\varepsilon\max_{C_\varepsilon}|g|\to0.\end{aligned}$$ 故 $\int_{C_\varepsilon}f\to-i\pi r$。把实轴上的区间 $[-R,x_0-\varepsilon]\cup[x_0+\varepsilon,R]$、大半圆与 $C_\varepsilon$ 组成围道；若上半平面只有有限个极点、实轴上的极点都是单极点且大弧消失，则 $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{PV}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx&=2\pi i\sum_{\operatorname{Im}z>0}\operatorname*{Res}f\\&\quad+\pi i\sum_{x_0\in\mathbb R}\operatorname*{Res}_{x_0}f,\end{aligned}$$ 实轴上的单极点只贡献「半留数」。若实轴上的极点是二阶或更高，$\int_{C_\varepsilon}$ 一般像 $\varepsilon^{1-m}$ 发散；即使主值因对称性存在，也不能直接套用上面的半留数公式。

分支切割与钥匙孔围道。计算 $I=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}/(1+x)\,dx$（$0<\alpha<1$）。取 $f(z)=z^{\alpha-1}/(1+z)$，在 $\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$ 上取分支 $0<\arg z<2\pi$，则 $f$ 单值全纯。围道由大圆 $|z|=R$、正实轴上沿（$\arg z=0$，从 $\varepsilon$ 到 $R$）、小圆 $|z|=\varepsilon$、正实轴下沿（$\arg z=2\pi$，从 $R$ 到 $\varepsilon$）组成。围道内只有单极点 $z=-1$（此处 $\arg z=\pi$），留数为 $$\operatorname*{Res}_{z=-1}f=\frac{e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}}{1}=e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}.$$ 上沿贡献 $I$；下沿因 $z^{\alpha-1}=e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)}x^{\alpha-1}$ 且方向相反，贡献 $-e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)}I$。大圆上 $|f|\le R^{\alpha-1}/(R-1)$、弧长 $2\pi R$，故积分为 $O(R^{\alpha-1})\to0$（$\alpha<1$）；小圆上 $|f|\le\varepsilon^{\alpha-1}/(1-\varepsilon)$、弧长 $2\pi\varepsilon$，故为 $O(\varepsilon^\alpha)\to0$（$\alpha>0$）。于是 $$(1-e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)})I=2\pi i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}.$$ 化简 $1-e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)}=e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}(e^{-i\pi(\alpha-1)}-e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)})=2i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}\sin\pi\alpha$，因此 $$\begin{aligned}I&=\frac{2\pi i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}}{2i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}\sin\pi\alpha}\\&=\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi\alpha}.\end{aligned}$$ 关键条件是分支固定且 $0<\alpha<1$，它保证两端圆弧都消失；若 $\alpha\le0$ 或 $\alpha\ge1$，需另作处理（积分可能发散，或需用到无穷远留数）。

$\log$ 技巧与检查清单。设 $f$ 是有理函数，在 $[0,\infty)$ 上无极点（包括 $0$），且分母次数至少比分子次数高 $2$。取同样的钥匙孔围道与分支 $0<\arg z<2\pi$，对 $f(z)\log z$ 积分。上沿贡献 $\int_0^\infty f(x)\ln x\,dx$，下沿贡献 $-\int_0^\infty f(x)(\ln x+2\pi i)dx$，两者相加为 $-2\pi i\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx$。大圆上 $|f(z)\log z|=O(R^{-2}\ln R)$、弧长 $O(R)$，故贡献消失；小圆上若 $f$ 在 $0$ 全纯，则贡献为 $O(\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon)\to0$。留数定理给出 $$\begin{aligned}-2\pi i\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx&=2\pi i\sum_{\text{极点}}\operatorname*{Res}\left[f(z)\log z\right].\end{aligned}$$ 即 $$\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx=-\sum_{\text{极点}}\operatorname*{Res}\left[f(z)\log z\right].$$ 注意在 $z=-1$ 处 $\log z=i\pi$（不是 $-\pi i$），分支选错会使结果整体差一个常数。计算前按顺序核对：(i) 奇点是否孤立、是否落在围道上；(ii) 大弧用 $zf\to0$ 还是 Jordan 引理（$a>0$，上半平面）；(iii) 小弧是否只有单极点、是否需要取主值；(iv) 多值函数的分支与割线是否和围道一致；(v) 用下半平面或无穷远留数时符号是否校正。任一条不满足，公式不能直接套用。
en: Conditions for the residue theorem. Let $f$ be holomorphic in a simply connected domain $\Omega$ except for finitely many isolated singularities $z_1,\dots,z_m$, and let $\gamma\subset\Omega$ be a piecewise smooth simple closed curve, positively oriented (counterclockwise), not passing through any $z_j$. Then $$\begin{aligned}\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz&=2\pi i\sum_{z_j\text{ inside }\gamma}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f.\end{aligned}$$ Both hypotheses 'isolated' and 'finitely many' matter: a singularity on $\gamma$ may make the integral diverge, and infinitely many singularities with an accumulation point may make the residue sum non-convergent. The residue is the coefficient $a_{-1}$ in the Laurent expansion $f(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_n(z-z_j)^n$; for a pole of order $m$, $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f&=\frac{1}{(m-1)!}\\&\quad\times\lim_{z\to z_j}\frac{d^{m-1}}{dz^{m-1}}\left[(z-z_j)^m f(z)\right].\end{aligned}$$ For a multiply connected region, the inner boundaries must be included with reversed orientation so that the total contour winds positively around the region; one cannot apply the formula to the outer boundary alone.

Residue at infinity. Let $f$ be holomorphic for $|z|>R$ except possibly at $\infty$, with Laurent expansion $f(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}c_nz^n$. Define $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=\infty}f&=-c_{-1}\\&=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=\rho}f(z)\,dz\quad(\rho>R)\end{aligned}$$ where the circle is traversed counterclockwise. The minus sign comes from the fact that the positive orientation at $\infty$ is clockwise: with $w=1/z$, $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=\infty}f&=\operatorname*{Res}_{w=0}\left[-\frac{1}{w^2}f\left(\frac1w\right)\right].\end{aligned}$$ Consequently, if $f$ is meromorphic on the Riemann sphere $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ except at finitely many points, the sum of all residues, including the one at infinity, is zero: $$\sum_{z_j\in\mathbb C}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=z_j}f+\operatorname*{Res}_{z=\infty}f=0.$$ For example, $f(z)=1/z$ has $\operatorname*{Res}_{0}f=1$ and $c_{-1}=1$, so $\operatorname*{Res}_{\infty}f=-1$, and the sum is $0$. When evaluating $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}$ via the lower half-plane, the sign at infinity and the orientation must be tracked; one cannot mix it blindly with the upper half-plane formula.

Large arcs: two vanishing criteria. Let $C_R=\{Re^{i\theta}:0\le\theta\le\pi\}$ be the large semicircle in the upper half-plane. Without an oscillating factor, if $zf(z)\to0$ uniformly on $C_R$ (that is, $\max_{C_R}|zf(z)|\to0$), then $$\left|\int_{C_R}f(z)\,dz\right|\le\pi R\max_{C_R}|f(z)|=\pi\max_{C_R}|zf(z)|\to0.$$ With an oscillating factor $e^{iaz}$ ($a>0$), Jordan's lemma requires only that $f$ tend to $0$ uniformly on $C_R$: using $|e^{iaz}|=e^{-aR\sin\theta}$ and Jordan's inequality $\sin\theta\ge2\theta/\pi$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi/2$, $$\left|\int_{C_R}f(z)e^{iaz}dz\right|\le\frac{\pi}{a}\max_{C_R}|f(z)|\to0.$$ The hypotheses are $a>0$ and the upper half-plane; for $a<0$ use the lower half-plane (where $e^{iaz}=e^{-i|a|z}$ decays), adjusting the orientation. If $a=0$ or $f$ does not tend to $0$, Jordan's lemma does not apply.

Small arcs and principal values. Let $x_0\in\mathbb R$ be a simple pole of $f$ with residue $r$, so $f(z)=\frac{r}{z-x_0}+g(z)$ with $g$ holomorphic near $x_0$. Let $C_\varepsilon=\{x_0+\varepsilon e^{i\theta}:\pi\ge\theta\ge0\}$ be the small semicircle in the upper half-plane, running from $x_0-\varepsilon$ to $x_0+\varepsilon$ clockwise around the pole. Then $$\begin{aligned}\int_{C_\varepsilon}\frac{r}{z-x_0}dz&=r\int_\pi^0 i\,d\theta=-i\pi r,\\\left|\int_{C_\varepsilon}g(z)dz\right|&\le\pi\varepsilon\max_{C_\varepsilon}|g|\to0.\end{aligned}$$ Hence $\int_{C_\varepsilon}f\to-i\pi r$. Form the contour from $[-R,x_0-\varepsilon]\cup[x_0+\varepsilon,R]$, the large semicircle and $C_\varepsilon$. If $f$ has finitely many poles in the upper half-plane, every pole on the real axis is simple, and the large arc vanishes, then $$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{PV}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx&=2\pi i\sum_{\operatorname{Im}z>0}\operatorname*{Res}f\\&\quad+\pi i\sum_{x_0\in\mathbb R}\operatorname*{Res}_{x_0}f,\end{aligned}$$ so a simple pole on the real axis contributes only a 'half residue'. If the pole on the axis has order at least $2$, $\int_{C_\varepsilon}$ generally diverges like $\varepsilon^{1-m}$; even if the principal value happens to exist by symmetry, the half-residue formula above cannot be applied directly.

Branch cuts and the keyhole contour. Compute $I=\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}/(1+x)\,dx$ for $0<\alpha<1$. Take $f(z)=z^{\alpha-1}/(1+z)$ with the branch $0<\arg z<2\pi$ on $\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$, which makes $f$ single-valued and holomorphic. Use the keyhole contour: the large circle $|z|=R$, the upper bank of the positive real axis ($\arg z=0$, from $\varepsilon$ to $R$), the small circle $|z|=\varepsilon$, and the lower bank ($\arg z=2\pi$, from $R$ to $\varepsilon$). Inside there is only the simple pole $z=-1$ (where $\arg z=\pi$), with residue $$\operatorname*{Res}_{z=-1}f=\frac{e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}}{1}=e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}.$$ The upper bank contributes $I$; the lower bank contributes $-e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)}I$, because $z^{\alpha-1}=e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)}x^{\alpha-1}$ there and the direction is reversed. On the large circle $|f|\le R^{\alpha-1}/(R-1)$ and the arc length is $2\pi R$, so the integral is $O(R^{\alpha-1})\to0$ since $\alpha<1$; on the small circle $|f|\le\varepsilon^{\alpha-1}/(1-\varepsilon)$ and the arc length is $2\pi\varepsilon$, so it is $O(\varepsilon^\alpha)\to0$ since $\alpha>0$. Therefore $$(1-e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)})I=2\pi i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}.$$ Since $1-e^{2\pi i(\alpha-1)}=e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}(e^{-i\pi(\alpha-1)}-e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)})=2i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}\sin\pi\alpha$, we get $$\begin{aligned}I&=\frac{2\pi i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}}{2i e^{i\pi(\alpha-1)}\sin\pi\alpha}\\&=\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi\alpha}.\end{aligned}$$ The key conditions are the fixed branch and $0<\alpha<1$, which make both circular arcs vanish; for $\alpha\le0$ or $\alpha\ge1$ the arcs need separate treatment (the integral may diverge or require a residue at infinity).

The log trick and a checklist. Let $f$ be rational, with no poles on $[0,\infty)$ (including $0$), and with denominator degree at least numerator degree plus $2$. Use the same keyhole contour and the branch $0<\arg z<2\pi$, and integrate $f(z)\log z$. The upper bank contributes $\int_0^\infty f(x)\ln x\,dx$; the lower bank contributes $-\int_0^\infty f(x)(\ln x+2\pi i)dx$, so together they give $-2\pi i\int_0^\infty f(x)dx$. On the large circle $|f(z)\log z|=O(R^{-2}\ln R)$ and the arc length is $O(R)$, so the contribution vanishes; on the small circle, if $f$ is holomorphic at $0$, the contribution is $O(\varepsilon\ln\varepsilon)\to0$. The residue theorem gives $$\begin{aligned}-2\pi i\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx&=2\pi i\sum_{\text{poles}}\operatorname*{Res}\left[f(z)\log z\right].\end{aligned}$$ That is, $$\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx=-\sum_{\text{poles}}\operatorname*{Res}\left[f(z)\log z\right].$$ Note that at $z=-1$ one has $\log z=i\pi$ (not $-i\pi$); choosing the branch incorrectly shifts the result by a constant. Before computing, check in order: (i) are the singularities isolated and off the contour; (ii) does the large arc vanish via $zf\to0$ or via Jordan's lemma ($a>0$, upper half-plane); (iii) does the small arc involve only a simple pole, and is a principal value required; (iv) are the branch and cut consistent with the contour; (v) are the signs correct when using the lower half-plane or the residue at infinity. If any condition fails, the formula cannot be applied directly.
